title: Twin Beds
novel:
Ted and Robin, freshly broken up, decided to try [[twin beds|twin beds]] — two small beds side by side, like children at summer camp. "It's [[practical|practical]]," Ted said. "No [[awkward|awkward]] [[cuddling|cuddle]]."

Barney and Don, meanwhile, [[competed|compete]] for Robin's [[affection|affection]]. Don brought flowers. Barney brought a [[skywriting|skywriting]] plane. The sky read "ROBIN" in white smoke.

Robin was [[torn|torn]]. Don was kind. Barney was Barney — loud, shameless, and somehow [[endearing|endearing]].

Ted watched from his twin bed, feeling like a [[referee|referee]] in a game he no longer played. "Why don't you both just [[back off|back off]]?" he suggested.

They did not.

In the end, Robin chose Don. Barney [[pretended|pretend]] it did not hurt, then went home and stared at the empty sky where his message had been. Ted, lying in his narrow bed that night, understood something: some [[arrangements|arrangement]] kept people close, but not too close — and sometimes that was the kindest distance of all.

twin beds.en: two single beds placed side by side

cuddle.en: the act of holding someone close

compete.en: to try to win against someone else

skywriting.en: words written in the sky by a plane

torn.en: unable to choose between two things

endearing.en: making people feel fond of you

referee.en: a person who watches a game fairly

pretend.en: to act as if something is true when it is not

arrangement.en: a plan for how things are set up
